questions_and_answers.question: Which set of German consonants are usually voiced according to the notes?
What happens to g, b, d when they occur at the end of a word or are followed by a voiceless consonant?

answers.answer: They are pronounced as long vowels
They are replaced by p, t, k

questions_and_answers.question: Which German word is pronounced with a voiceless final consonant as described in the notes?
According to the notes, what helps when pronouncing pre-vocalic r clusters?

answers.answer: Inserting a vowel between the consonant and r

questions_and_answers.question: Which practice list belongs to the pre-vocalic r cluster section?
What does the article state about the German 'l' sound?

answers.answer: It is almost identical to the English 'l' sound

questions_and_answers.question: Which words does the article recommend practising to distinguish the German 'l' sound?
How should the 'l' be pronounced in German according to the notes?

answers.answer: Held for a full second after vowels

questions_and_answers.question: Why does the article suggest pronouncing German 'hohl' carefully?
Which practice list is given for words with the 'l' sound?

articles.text:
Notes on pronunciation
A. German b, g, d and p, t, k.
1. In most cases the symbols b, g, d and p, t, k represent the same sounds in German as in English. You probably experience little difficulty therefore in pronouncing the following words:
Bahnhof
aber
Pass
(Mappe)
danke
oder
Taxe
bitte
ist
gut
sagen
kann
Ecke
Bank
b, g, d usually represent what we call voiced sounds: that is, your vocal cords are vibrating when you make these sounds. p, t, k represent what we call voiceless sounds: that is, your vocal cords are not vibrating, and you are actually whispering when you make these sounds.
2. However, b, g, d also represent the voiceless sounds when they occur at the end of a word or syllable and when they are followed by other voiceless sounds:
abheben "ap-heben"
bleibt "bleip-t"
hebt … ab "hep-t … ap"
glaubt "glaup-t"
siebzehn "siep-zehn"
gibt "gip-t"
sind "sin-t"
und "unt"
Flughafen "Fluk-hafen"
zeigt "zeik-t"
Tag "Tak"
sagt "sak-t"
This is especially important to realize when considering verb forms. Since there is an alternation between voiced and voiceless endings (-e, -en, -t) many verbs actually have alternate stems which the writing system does not show. bleib- or "bleip-" (bleibe) (bleibt).

B. Pre-vocalic r in clusters. Practice 1.
sag- (sage)
or "sak-" (sagt).
Frau

As noted in Unit 2 you may find it easier to break up the cluster by inserting a vowel between the initial consonant and the r. This may be more necessary in the following group where the r is voiced. For rei try saying darei for example, and for bringen, baringen, etc.

Practice 2.
drei
dringen
Adresse

braun
bringen
Gebrauch
verbrennen

Greis

C. Pre-vocalic r after vowels and initially. Practice 3.

D. The German l.
Bahre
Zigarre
Ehre
ihre
Maria
beraten
erreichen
gerieben
Rat
reich
Rind
roh
Pronounce English "leap" and "believe". Ask your instructor to pronounce German lieb and belieben. In these words the l sound is almost identical in both languages. Remember of course that the German ie sound is higher and tenser than the English vowel, and this difference is reflected somewhat in the l.
Practice 4:
Lied
lesen
leider
Lack
Loch
lösen
lud
lügen
beleben
Geleit
gelogen
beluden
Ask your instructor to pronounce German lieb again slowly and repeat it after him as slowly as you can, holding the l for a full second or more. Then say the l alone just the same way. This is the only l sound which occurs in German. It is the same sound before and after vowels. After vowels however it occurs almost as a separate syllable. Now ask your instructor to pronounce German hohl. You will note that this word does not sound like English "hole". Listen carefully and see if you can distinguish the two syllables, the l syllable and the l syllable, as your instructor says hohl again. In the following exercise try to imitate him exactly.
